Apple opens the door to a nightmare world of always-listening tech
articles.body:
Watch what you say: Apple opens the door to a nightmare world of always-listening tech
Apple this week announced plans to roll out "always-listening" features for newer Apple Watches. One of the features, Live Rewind, lets you "go back in time" and replay the most recent 15 seconds of ambient audio as a text transcript. The other feature, Siri Recap, listens throughout the day and summarizes your conversations as high-level notes into a written report on your iPhone.
Apple claims these features are helpful to "jog" your memory. The massive trade-off is that your Apple Watch is always listening to you and anyone else within earshot while the feature is enabled.
Here's the relevant section from Apple's live event:
Given these features we're bound to be controversial, it's clear that Apple put thought into the security and privacy guardrails before shipping these features (which may still change). The tech giant says on its support page that the always-listening tech doesn't record or store audio, and that the recaps are end-to-end encrypted so that any summarized data is inaccessible to anyone else, not even Apple. And, its security documentation [PDF] detailing how the features work is worth reading as well.
What is more concerning to me, to underscore on a point I made in a Bluesky post, is that Apple is opening the door to a world where other companies, device makers, and app developers try to recreate or rival Apple's technology and do a far shoddier job, all the while creating a worse surveillance monster and introducing new security and privacy risks along the way.
So far there have been a few companies and startups that made always-listening devices, like pendants, often including AI. Apple by comparison is one of the largest technology companies in the world and its global reach means millions of people will get these features and switch them on. Apple's market dominance, coupled with its decision to make always-listening tech, sets a precedent that signals it's OK for other companies to follow suit and normalize this intrusive tech. It also implies that there is money to be made in developing this technology, making it a space ripe for disruption (or exploitation) by profiteers.
Bloomberg ($) reports lawyers are already finding that Apple's always-listening tech is at odds with the law in several U.S. states. Some states require all parties' consent before being recorded, setting up the feature for potential legal battles down the line. This comes amid the rise of smart camera-enabled "pervert glasses" like those made by Meta and Snap, which have supercharged abuse and harassment against people by recording them without consent.
~this week in security~ is my weekly cybersecurity newsletter and blog supported by readers like you. Please consider signing up for a paid subscription starting at $10/month for access to exclusive articles, analysis, and more.
Or, you can submit a one-time tip or gift a paid subscription to show your support!
Recent stories include: How residential proxy networks are hiding hackers in your home | The top highlights from Black Hat, Def Con, and BSides Las Vegas 2026 | When AI chatbots and LLMs get legal, check your privilege | Vigilantism comes for Flock
Privacy for me, but not for thee?
While Apple has emphasized security and privacy features for its own users, it hasn't explained how people opt out of its customers' recordings.
I chatted this week with Em, a digital privacy and security technologist, activist, and author of the Control Alt Delete blog, and whose work you have no doubt seen while she wrote for Privacy Guides. Em told me that these new Apple features follow a "recent trend of gadgets that are constantly collecting information from surroundings, including from people who aren't wearing or buying these gadgets themselves," like smart glasses and speakers.
Em said that while anyone can make notes of every conversation they have, this kind of technology "normalizes it happening at all time and in every context."
"Even if Apple seems to have put some thought into protecting the privacy and consent of the people using the Apple Watch, this technology doesn't do much to protect the privacy and consent of everyone interacting with people using it," Em told me.
I also asked Thorin Klosowski, a senior security and privacy activist at Electronic Frontier Foundation, for his thoughts and he said similarly that Apple's approach is largely about protecting its customers' data but does little for anyone else.
"Increasingly we’re seeing tech companies frame privacy this way — as personal responsibility — but it has never been just about that, it’s a collective effort that relies as much on personal choice as it does social contracts," said Klosowski. He added that we should all be free to converse without fear of tech documenting everything that's being said. "Especially when combined with all the other similar devices we’re seeing, whether that’s pendants or glasses or rings, there is absolutely a risk of normalization here."
EFF's privacy litigation director Adam Schwartz added that since there's no practical means for people to consent or decline recording, "we suggest people should think twice before using this technology, out of respect to the conversational privacy of others."
For its part, Apple says on its support page that users should "consider those around you where conversations may be private or sensitive." The broader message Apple seems to be sending is: Prepare for a world where everyday devices are always listening in.

articles.title: Fujifilm To Boost Tape Production 5x As AI Fuels Archiving Demand
articles.body:
Fujifilm To Boost Tape Production 5x As AI Fuels Archiving Demand (arstechnica.com) 41
			
		 	
				An anonymous reader quotes a report from Ars Technica: In an announcement released Thursday, Fujifilm said it will invest roughly 10 billion yen (about $63 million) to increase its production capacity fivefold for an unlikely beneficiary of the AI era: magnetic tape. Fujifilm attributes the surge in archiving demand to the spread of generative AI, which the company remarked is producing "exponential growth" in data needs worldwide. The 5x increase in production capacity will be measured against fiscal year 2025 production levels.
The investment in Fujifilm's Kanagawa Factory, Odawara site will make it "the largest investment Fujifilm has made to date in dedicated LTO tape facilities." The project will run from fiscal years 2026 through 2028 to fund manufacturing expansion and additional personnel, primarily to produce the latest-generation "FUJIFILM LTO Ultrium10" tape. [...]
According to Fujifilm, "major cloud service and data center operators" have been expanding their use of magnetic tape because it can store large data volumes at relatively low cost. Tape backups can be easily disconnected and stored in a drawer, a vault, or a separate facility. Fujifilm highlights the ability to air-gap tape cartridges as a last defense for user data: "Given the sophistication of cyberattacks, magnetic tape is attracting increasing attention as a means of protecting data from threats such as ransomware."

articles.title: US midterm elections 2026 live updates: Democrats win Senate control and edge
articles.body:
This live blog is now closed. You can follow our latest midterms election coverage here:
History made in races across the US – as it happened
Democrats flip Senate seats in Texas, Iowa, Kansas, North Carolina, South Carolina and Ohio; voters reject Trump’s agenda in ‘blue wave’
Wed 4 Nov 2026 07.24 EST
First published on Tue 3 Nov 2026 17.49 EST
Wed 4 Nov 2026 07.24 EST
First published on Tue 3 Nov 2026 17.49 EST
Summary of midterm results so far
The Democratic party has taken control of Congress in a major setback for Donald Trump and Republicans. Here are some of the key results, historic victories and political developments from the midterm elections so far:
- The Democrats have secured 228 seats in the House (with 218 needed for a majority) and 54 seats in the Senate (with 51 needed for control). The party has flipped at least seven Senate seats in red states and battlegrounds, including Kansas – which hasn’t elected a Democratic senator in nearly a century – Iowa, Texas, Ohio, Maine, North Carolina and South Carolina. In the House, the Democrats have flipped more than two dozen districts.
- History was made in Michigan as Democrat Abdul El-Sayed, an Egptian American doctor, became the first Muslim ever elected to the US Senate, beating Republican Mike Rogers for the key battleground seat. “You took a chance on the unlikeliest of candidates,” El-Sayed said in his election night speech.
- Other seismic wins in federal and state races for the Democrats include James Talarico, who became the first Democrat in 38 years to win a US Senate seat in Texas; Adam Hamilton, who is now the first Democrat to win a US Senate seat in Kansas since 1932; and progressive Troy Jackson, who unseated Susan Collins in Maine, ending her 30-year career in the US Senate.
- Democrat Aaron Ford won the race for governor in Nevada, toppling Republican incumbent Joe Lombardo and becoming the state’s first black governor.
- Donald Trump said he was “absolutely willing to accept those results” in an interview with the New York Times. He added: “We’ll, you know, look forward to working with them [Democrats] … We’ll probably work something out.”
- Former US president Barack Obama has welcomed the midterm election results as a clear rejection of divisive politics. “Tonight, the American people sent a clear message – they want a politics that brings people together rather than divides them, and leaders who offer concrete solutions to the challenges they face,” he said.
Read our full report here:
Fox News host Sean Hannity, one of Donald Trump’s most prominent supporters in conservative media, has acknowledged that the scale of public “hatred” towards the US president contributed to the Republicans’ heavy midtern election losses.
“Hatred is a hell of a motivator,” he told fellow panellist Harold Ford Jr.
He added: “I think the hatred for this man is unprecedented. I’ve never seen anything like it.”
In another historic first, the Democrats are projected to win Nevada’s second congressional district for the first time since its creation in 1981.
Democrat Teresa Benitez-Thompson is in the lead ahead of Republican David Flippo, although the race has not yet been called by the Associated Press.
If she holds on to that lead and flips the House seat, it will mark the first time since 1947 that Nevada has had an all-Democrat congressional delegation. Democrat incumbents have swept all of Nevada’s three remaining House seats, whose races have been called by AP.
“One of the biggest upsets in Nevada history, a district never held by a Democrat in its 45 years of existence,” said Jon Ralston, founder and CEO of the Nevada Independent, of Benitez-Thompson’s projected win.
Democrat James Talarico has won the US Senate race in Texas, breaking a 38-year drought for his party in the Republican stronghold and delivering a stunning blow to Donald Trump.
Talarico defeated Republican Ken Paxton, the state attorney general and a staunch ally of the US president, in one of the most closely watched contests of the midterm elections to decide control of Congress.
“We just took back Texas!” the 37-year-old told jubilant supporters at an election night party in Austin, the state capital and his home city. “We just proved that all the money in the world is no match for the people of Texas. We have just shown that a politics of division is no match for a politics of love.”
Read more:
Democrat Aaron Ford makes history as Nevada elects its first black governor
Nevada has elected Democrat Aaron Ford as its next governor, making him the first black person to hold the office in the state’s history.
His win toppled the Republican incumbent Joe Lombardo in a closely watched race, and delivered an important victory for the Democrats in one of the country’s key battleground states.
Ford ran his campaign with the backing of California governor Gavin Newsom and former vice-president Kamala Harris, focusing on the cost of living, housing affordability and student debt.
Opinion: The death knell of Trumpism has finally sounded
There’s a certain freedom in low expectations. Going in to Tuesday’s midterm elections, forecasts were so grim for the Republicans that poll watchers started trading a kind of knowing joke: that the results would either mean the end of the Trump era, or the end of the polling profession.
Amid those sorts of predictions, any Republican victories would have seemed like a minor miracle. The expectation was that Democrats would have a blowout; Republicans, counting on the final tally to be a bit more mixed, would therefore almost certainly have the freedom to claim that they’d done better than anyone had thought they would.
It will be difficult to credit those spins today. The electorate issued the president a message of dissatisfaction with the second Trump term, and voted decisively to curb his power.
Now, with a Senate majority, Democrats will be able to investigate the president and his cabinet members, draw public attention to their own agenda items, assert Congress’s constitutional prerogatives, and block Republican judicial appointments.
In the coming days and weeks, Trump will alternately say that the Republican losses were fake – the result of fraud by a nefarious but ill-defined conspiracy of Democrats and illegal immigrants – and that they were real, but somebody else’s fault.
His administration has signaled over the past weeks that it could make efforts to contest the certification of especially close Senate races, notably Alaska.
But the wind may have gone out of the sails of that plan for now: for what it’s worth, which isn’t much, Trump told the New York Times on Tuesday night that he would accept the results of the midterms. What’s certain is that he will rail into microphones and complain in all caps on social media. But it is not likely that any of that will go anywhere. Because Tuesday night – almost exactly 10 years after he won the presidency in an upset victory over Hillary Clinton in 2016 – the Trump era effectively came to an end.
Read more:
'The American people sent a clear message,' says Obama
Former US president Barack Obama has welcomed the midterm election results as a clear rejection of divisive politics.
In a statement on X, he said:
 Tonight, the American people sent a clear message – they want a politics that brings people together rather than divides them, and leaders who offer concrete solutions to the challenges they face.
These results were only possible because outstanding candidates stepped forward in every region of the country – including in areas once considered long shots. They came from different backgrounds and represented a range of political perspectives, but were united by shared values, a belief in public service, and a commitment to putting the people of their districts and states first.”
Spain’s socialist prime minister, Pedro Sánchez – who has been Donald Trump’s most vociferous European critic – is celebrating last night’s results, hailing them as proof of a progressive fightback and of the “crumbling” of what he called the “ultra wave”.
“Yesterday, the American people voted against policies that only serve to impoverish people,” he posted on X. “Against hate. Against sexism. Against climate denialism and against the privileges of the elites.”
Sánchez, who faces an uphill battle to secure another term in office in Spain’s general election at the end of the month, added: “It happened in Brazil. It just happened in the US. And it will happen soon in Spain.”
Democrat Tina Kotek wins re-election for governor in Oregon
The incumbent Democratic governor of Oregon, Tina Kotek, has won her re-election bid against Republican Christine Drazan.
It is the second time Kotek has defeated Drazan, after the two faced off in the 2022 governor race.
Republican Pete Ricketts wins re-election in Nebraska Senate race
Republican senator Pete Ricketts has won his re-election bid in Nebraska, defeating independent candidate Dan Osborn.
Ricketts, a former Nebraska governor, was appointed to the Senate in 2023 to replace Republican senator Ben Sasse and won a special election in 2024 to serve the final two years of his predecessor’s term.
History was made in Michigan as Abdul El-Sayed, an Egptian American doctor, became the first Muslim ever elected to the US Senate, beating Mike Rogers for the key battleground seat.
His victory is all the more remarkable given the ugly campaign of anti-Muslim rhetoric that sought to undermine his candidacy, led by Donald Trump and his Republican allies.
The Democrat’s faith was weaponised throughout the race, with Trump calling him a “jihadist” and Rogers questioning his loyalty to the US. El-Sayed met the attacks with defiance, telling Trump that he could “just go on and call me senator after November”.
In his victory speech, El-Sayed told a jubilant crowd:
 My name is Abdulrahman Mohamed El-Sayed, and I am so proud and honoured to stand here as your Senator-elect from the great state of Michigan.
Up until right about now, you might have noticed I always say inshallah, or God willing, whenever the outcome of this race was mentioned. But today, tonight, we can turn that inshallah into an alhamdulillah (praise be to God).”
My colleague Joseph Gedeon has more:
Latest midterm results - at a glance
It’s 3am ET in Washington/8am GMT, and as people start seeing their phones ping with notifications, here are where things stand at the moment.
- Democrats have won control of Congress in a stunning rebuke of Donald Trump’s agenda, delivering an astonishing result and a widely predicted “blue wave” across the country. As of now, Democrats have clinched 54 seats in the Senate (they needed 51 to reclaim the majority) and 225 House seats (they needed 218 to take control of the lower chamber). We’re still awaiting the results for several races – namely in Alaska.
- There were several seismic and historic wins in federal and state races for Democrats. James Talarico became the first Democrat in 38 years to win a US Senate seat in Texas; Adam Hamilton is now the first Democrat to win a US Senate seat in Kansas since 1932; In Maine, progressive Troy Jackson unseated Susan Collins after a thirty-year grip on the state’s US Senate seat; and Abdul El-Sayed won the US senate race in Michigan – one of the cycle’s most closely watched competitions.
- We’re waiting on a number of nail-biting races to be called. The race for US Senate in Mississippi is extremely close, and could see a Democratic upset, and it’s still to early to call the Senate contest in Alaska.
- Democrats also made history in a number of gubernatorial races. Keisha Lance Bottoms’ victory in Georgia means that she will be the first Black female governor in US history. Gina Hinojosa makes history as Texas’ first Latina governor, and the first Democrat to occupy the governor’s mansion since 1990. Meanwhile, David Crowley became Wisconsin’s first Black governor after winning his race tonight.
- Donald Trump said he was “absolutely willing to accept those results” in an interview with the New York Times. He added: “We’ll, you know, look forward to working with them [Democrats] … We’ll probably work something out.”

“One of the biggest upsets in Nevada history, a district never held by a Democrat in its 45 years of existence,” said Jon Ralston, founder and CEO of the Nevada Independent, of Benitez-Thompson’s projected win.
Democrat James Talarico has won the US Senate race in Texas, breaking a 38-year drought for his party in the Republican stronghold and delivering a stunning blow to Donald Trump.
Talarico defeated Republican Ken Paxton, the state attorney general and a staunch ally of the US president, in one of the most closely watched contests of the midterm elections to decide control of Congress.
“We just took back Texas!” the 37-year-old told jubilant supporters at an election night party in Austin, the state capital and his home city. “We just proved that all the money in the world is no match for the people of Texas. We have just shown that a politics of division is no match for a politics of love.”
Read more:
Democrat Aaron Ford makes history as Nevada elects its first black governor
Nevada has elected Democrat Aaron Ford as its next governor, making him the first black person to hold the office in the state’s history.
His win toppled the Republican incumbent Joe Lombardo in a closely watched race, and delivered an important victory for the Democrats in one of the country’s key battleground states.
Ford ran his campaign with the backing of California governor Gavin Newsom and former vice-president Kamala Harris, focusing on the cost of living, housing affordability and student debt.
Opinion: The death knell of Trumpism has finally sounded
There’s a certain freedom in low expectations. Going in to Tuesday’s midterm elections, forecasts were so grim for the Republicans that poll watchers started trading a kind of knowing joke: that the results would either mean the end of the Trump era, or the end of the polling profession.
Amid those sorts of predictions, any Republican victories would have seemed like a minor miracle. The expectation was that Democrats would have a blowout; Republicans, counting on the final tally to be a bit more mixed, would therefore almost certainly have the freedom to claim that they’d done better than anyone had thought they would.
It will be difficult to credit those spins today. The electorate issued the president a message of dissatisfaction with the second Trump term, and voted decisively to curb his power.
Now, with a Senate majority, Democrats will be able to investigate the president and his cabinet members, draw public attention to their own agenda items, assert Congress’s constitutional prerogatives, and block Republican judicial appointments.
In the coming days and weeks, Trump will alternately say that the Republican losses were fake – the result of fraud by a nefarious but ill-defined conspiracy of Democrats and illegal immigrants – and that they were real, but somebody else’s fault.
His administration has signaled over the past weeks that it could make efforts to contest the certification of especially close Senate races, notably Alaska.
But the wind may have gone out of the sails of that plan for now: for what it’s worth, which isn’t much, Trump told the New York Times on Tuesday night that he would accept the results of the midterms. What’s certain is that he will rail into microphones and complain in all caps on social media. But it is not likely that any of that will go anywhere. Because Tuesday night – almost exactly 10 years after he won the presidency in an upset victory over Hillary Clinton in 2016 – the Trump era effectively came to an end.
Read more:
'The American people sent a clear message,' says Obama
Former US president Barack Obama has welcomed the midterm election results as a clear rejection of divisive politics.
In a statement on X, he said:
 Tonight, the American people sent a clear message – they want a politics that brings people together rather than divides them, and leaders who offer concrete solutions to the challenges they face.
These results were only possible because outstanding candidates stepped forward in every region of the country – including in areas once considered long shots. They came from different backgrounds and represented a range of political perspectives, but were united by shared values, a belief in public service, and a commitment to putting the people of their districts and states first.”
Spain’s socialist prime minister, Pedro Sánchez – who has been Donald Trump’s most vociferous European critic – is celebrating last night’s results, hailing them as proof of a progressive fightback and of the “crumbling” of what he called the “ultra wave”.
“Yesterday, the American people voted against policies that only serve to impoverish people,” he posted on X. “Against hate. Against sexism. Against climate denialism and against the privileges of the elites.”
Sánchez, who faces an uphill battle to secure another term in office in Spain’s general election at the end of the month, added: “It happened in Brazil. It just happened in the US. And it will happen soon in Spain.”
Democrat Tina Kotek wins re-election for governor in Oregon
The incumbent Democratic governor of Oregon, Tina Kotek, has won her re-election bid against Republican Christine Drazan.
It is the second time Kotek has defeated Drazan, after the two faced off in the 2022 governor race.
Republican Pete Ricketts wins re-election in Nebraska Senate race
Republican senator Pete Ricketts has won his re-election bid in Nebraska, defeating independent candidate Dan Osborn.
Ricketts, a former Nebraska governor, was appointed to the Senate in 2023 to replace Republican senator Ben Sasse and won a special election in 2024 to serve the final two years of his predecessor’s term.
History was made in Michigan as Abdul El-Sayed, an Egptian American doctor, became the first Muslim ever elected to the US Senate, beating Mike Rogers for the key battleground seat.
His victory is all the more remarkable given the ugly campaign of anti-Muslim rhetoric that sought to undermine his candidacy, led by Donald Trump and his Republican allies.
The Democrat’s faith was weaponised throughout the race, with Trump calling him a “jihadist” and Rogers questioning his loyalty to the US. El-Sayed met the attacks with defiance, telling Trump that he could “just go on and call me senator after November”.
In his victory speech, El-Sayed told a jubilant crowd:
 My name is Abdulrahman Mohamed El-Sayed, and I am so proud and honoured to stand here as your Senator-elect from the great state of Michigan.
Up until right about now, you might have noticed I always say inshallah, or God willing, whenever the outcome of this race was mentioned. But today, tonight, we can turn that inshallah into an alhamdulillah (praise be to God).”
My colleague Joseph Gedeon has more:
Latest midterm results - at a glance
It’s 3am ET in Washington/8am GMT, and as people start seeing their phones ping with notifications, here are where things stand at the moment.
- Democrats have won control of Congress in a stunning rebuke of Donald Trump’s agenda, delivering an astonishing result and a widely predicted “blue wave” across the country. As of now, Democrats have clinched 54 seats in the Senate (they needed 51 to reclaim the majority) and 225 House seats (they needed 218 to take control of the lower chamber). We’re still awaiting the results for several races – namely in Alaska.
- There were several seismic and historic wins in federal and state races for Democrats. James Talarico became the first Democrat in 38 years to win a US Senate seat in Texas; Adam Hamilton is now the first Democrat to win a US Senate seat in Kansas since 1932; In Maine, progressive Troy Jackson unseated Susan Collins after a thirty-year grip on the state’s US Senate seat; and Abdul El-Sayed won the US senate race in Michigan – one of the cycle’s most closely watched competitions.
- We’re waiting on a number of nail-biting races to be called. The race for US Senate in Mississippi is extremely close, and could see a Democratic upset, and it’s still to early to call the Senate contest in Alaska.
- Democrats also made history in a number of gubernatorial races. Keisha Lance Bottoms’ victory in Georgia means that she will be the first Black female governor in US history. Gina Hinojosa makes history as Texas’ first Latina governor, and the first Democrat to occupy the governor’s mansion since 1990. Meanwhile, David Crowley became Wisconsin’s first Black governor after winning his race tonight.
- Donald Trump said he was “absolutely willing to accept those results” in an interview with the New York Times. He added: “We’ll, you know, look forward to working with them [Democrats] … We’ll probably work something out.”

articles.title: Coffee's new status symbol is a machine without plastic
articles.body:
For decades, it was all the bells and whistles that was the selling point for a fancy coffee machine. Now, consumers are looking for what it lacks.
Growing concern over microplastics and sustainability is sparking a wave of plastic-free coffee pods and machines.
Coffee companies and appliance makers have released new machines and redesigned capsules in recent months. Keurig and Lavazza’s new pods ditch the traditional plastic cups for compostable coffee tablets. Caraway’s new machine uses traditional coffee grounds, but unlike a conventional drip machine, the stainless steel and glass machine doesn’t have plastic in its brew path.
More research is needed to determine the actual harm microplastics cause. But nine in 10 Americans are concerned about the effect of the minuscule plastic pieces on the planet and their bodies, according to a 2025 poll conducted by environmental group 5 Gyres; and studies have shown that pods shed microplastics.
The growth in pricey equipment and plastic-free pods fits a broader pattern of consumers trading up on home coffee equipment since the pandemic, said Peter Giuliano, senior adviser for research at Specialty Coffee Association.
The appeal and growth combine three things: health worries about microplastics, concern about plastic in the environment and the “feeling that metal and glass are more ‘luxury’ than plastic,” he told CNN.
New pods
In June, Lavazza introduced Tablì in the US, a $129 machine that uses only single-serve espresso tablets made with compressed ground coffee — a shift from its capsules made from plastic and aluminum.
The tablets are made by a custom technology that “compresses precisely dosed, ground, and tamped coffee into a solid, ready-to-use tab,” Lavazza said in a press release.
The Italian company says the new machine is its “largest investment yet” in the United States as it looks to double revenue to $1 billion by 2029, unlocking the stranglehold Keurig Dr. Pepper has on the coffee market.
Tablì is aimed at customers who want a sustainable alternative to the traditional pod, according to Daniele Foti, vice president of marketing for Lavazza North America.
“Consumers want to enjoy their coffee without the waste that usually comes with single-serve,” he told CNN.
Keurig, which ushered in the boom of plastics with their K-Cups back in the 1990s, launched in October a new line of compostable pods with a specially designed machine called the Alta. (The new pods don’t fit in the old machines.)
Called AltaRounds, the pods have been in development since 2020 in response to consumers’ shifting sustainability and health preferences.
The new pods represent a “significant reduction in plastic compared to our K-Cup pods,” said Phil Drapeau, senior vice president for Keurig’s Future Coffee Systems unit.
“We’ve heard clearly from customers that they want more sustainable products and specifically less plastic and plastic waste,” Drapeau told CNN. “Our data shows that drink variety, quality, and less plastic waste are high priorities across almost every group.”
Keurig has come under fire in the past over its pods, agreeing in 2022 to pay $10 million to settle a class-action lawsuit alleging it misled consumers by marketing its plastic K-Cups as recyclable, though it denied any wrongdoing.
But while the pods and the machine contain less plastic, they are considerably more expensive than a traditional Keurig machine. The Alta bundle that includes glassware and pods costs $499.
Melissa Valliant, director of communications for 5 Gyres, said that both the Lavazza and Keurig products still use plastic packaging, which “ends up in a landfill, incinerator, or our environment after use, contributing to the planet’s growing plastic pollution crisis.”
New machine
Caraway has focused on developing a $495 coffee machine, released last month, that’s created entirely of stainless steel and glass, ensuring that no plastic touches the ground coffee. (Lavazza’s and Keurig’s machines contain some amounts of plastic.)
Developing a coffee machine with plastic-free brew path was challenging, according to Caraway CEO Jordan Nathan. That’s because the pricey glass and steel parts all need to be custom-made.
“We had to make the best coffee possible with no plastic on the interior with a full metal body, but also in a small (counter) footprint that had a single dial,” he told CNN.
Concern over plastic in the kitchen and its affects on the endocrine system has been growing for the past few years, Nathan said, referencing a viral article that linked black plastics in the kitchen to alarming levels of toxic flame retardants.
Social media, influencers and various scientific studies have all fueled the conversation, with parents and other health-conscious shoppers avoiding plastic where they can, including in makeup, food and bedding. Caraway’s other plastic-free products, like cutting boards, have soared in sales over the past three years.
Coffee is a natural next step, Nathan added, because “you never want to heat plastic.”
Demand for Caraway’s new 10-cup coffee maker has been so strong that it’s sold out until January, forcing the company to ramp up production. Meanwhile, Keurig and Lavazza reported similar interest with both company’s product selling out quickly after their initial release.
That appetite for these pods and machines signals the industry will move toward more plastic-free alternatives, Nathan said.
“If you’re not doing it, you’re behind where the puck is moving,” he concluded.

articles.title: Distinct cellular and genetic differences in colorectal cancer in young patients
articles.body:
Study reveals distinct cellular and genetic differences in colorectal cancer in younger patients
Researchers identified age-associated differences in tumor composition and gene activity, creating a foundation for investigating why colorectal cancer can be more aggressive in younger adults
Dana-Farber Cancer Institute researchers, along with Mass General Brigham researchers from the Gene Lay Institute of Immunology and Inflammation, and the Broad Institute, have uncovered biological clues to why colorectal cancer can behave more aggressively in younger people. Published today in Nature Medicine, the study — the largest of its kind — lays a foundation for understanding age-associated differences in colorectal cancer and exploring future treatments.
In the United States, colorectal cancer diagnosis rates among people younger than 50 rose 2.9% per year from 2013 through 2022, according to the American Cancer Society. Its 2026 report identifies colorectal cancer as the leading cause of cancer death in this age group. Younger patients are also more likely to be diagnosed at advanced stages, underscoring the need to better understand the biology of early-onset disease.
"Through Dana-Farber’s Young-Onset Colorectal Cancer Center, we see how profoundly this disease can affect younger patients and their families, often during the busiest and most formative years of life," said co-senior author Kimmie Ng, MD, MPH, who is the director of the Young-Onset Colorectal Cancer Center at Dana-Farber. "This collaborative work with Mass General Brigham researchers from the Gene Lay Institute and researchers from the Broad Institute gives us important new insight into the biology of these tumors. The findings provide a valuable roadmap for further investigating the distinct features of young-onset colorectal cancer. Our ultimate goal is to discover novel strategies for prevention, diagnosis, and treatment for our young patients."
"The need to understand why colorectal cancer is affecting younger adults at increasing rates is urgent," said co-senior author Ana C. Anderson, PhD, a core faculty member of the Gene Lay Institute of Immunology and Inflammation at Brigham and Women’s Hospital, Massachusetts General Hospital, and Harvard Medical School. "And that starts with understanding the biology of the disease across the entire lifespan. By looking beyond conventional age cutoffs, we’ve uncovered biological patterns that earlier studies may have missed and created a foundation for the field to investigate them further. While we’re still at the beginning of understanding what these differences mean, our work gives researchers a new direction to pursue in tackling this urgent problem in human disease."
The research team, led by first author Caroline Porter, PhD, of the Klarman Cell Observatory at the Broad Institute, studied specimens from surgeries stored in Dana-Farber’s Gastrointestinal Biobank from surgeries at Brigham and Women’s Hospital. Co-senior authors include Anderson, Ng, and Ramnik J. Xavier, MD, PhD, of the Broad Institute, Mass General Brigham, and the Gene Lay Institute. They analyzed 189 tumors from patients ages 29 to 90+, including 54 diagnosed before age 50, and 135 diagnosed at age 50 or older. Using a technique called single-nucleus RNA sequencing, the researchers measured gene activity in more than 850,000 cancer cells and other cells in the tumors. The technique, which works with frozen tissue, enabled the team to build a detailed map of tumor cells by studying archived samples with extensive clinical record data.
Rather than dividing the tumor samples into two data sets and comparing the younger and older age groups, the researchers looked for factors that changed gradually with age, accounting for tumor location, stage, sex, and prior treatment in their analyses. This approach revealed subtle differences that likely would have been obscured by a simple two-data set comparison.
Among tumors of the most common colorectal cancer subtype, younger patients’ tumors had a significantly higher proportion of connective and supporting cells relative to cancer cells. A higher proportion of connective and supporting cells has been linked to chemotherapy resistance in several types of solid cancer. The team confirmed this pattern using gene-activity data from 564 other tumors and computer analysis of stained tissue images from another 712 tumors.
Younger patients also had higher activity of long non-coding RNAs, molecules that can regulate genes without making proteins. Some appeared repeatedly across different types of cancer cells. Many are "dark" RNAs, whose functions remain largely unknown. The team also saw gene activity suggesting stronger signaling between cells that can help cancer cells move and invade nearby tissue in younger patients.
"Our study is an advance from previous work in that we analyzed tumors from a large number of patients and used single-cell approaches to find novel features unique to tumors from young patients," said Xavier, a co-senior author of the study, a core institute member at the Broad Institute, Kurt Isselbacher Professor at Massachusetts General Hospital and Harvard Medical School, and Vice Director of the Gene Lay Institute. Xavier is also a gastroenterologist at Mass General Brigham. "This work sets the stage for future mechanistic studies on how these cell programs interact with chemicals from the diet and from gut microbes to cause early-onset colorectal cancer."
Although the findings provide key insight into colorectal cancer in young individuals, they do not yet provide proof that these differences cause more aggressive disease. One remaining question is whether there are differences in immune responses in these tumors across ages — the researchers' methods captured relatively few immune cells. Future studies will explore how these changes may affect cancer growth and spread, and whether they offer opportunities for prevention or treatment.

Brais, Jennifer S. Thalappillil, Marios Giannakis, Ramnik J. Xavier, Ana C. Anderson and Kimmie Ng.

Ogino has served as a consultant for Sanofi Pasteur. Xavier is a co-founder of Convergence Bio, a scientific advisory board member at Nestlé and Magnet BioMedicine, and a board director at MoonLake Immunotherapeutics; these organizations had no role in the study. Deguine is a member of BioRender’s scientific advisory board. Giannakis receives institutional research funding from Janssen and Sunbird Bio, has consulted for Nerviano Medical Sciences, and has received honoraria from OncLive and PER. Ng consults for or serves on advisory boards for Bayer, Pfizer, CytomX, Jazz Pharmaceuticals, Revolution Medicines, Agenus, Johnson & Johnson, AbbVie, Sanofi, GlaxoSmithKline, Flagship Pioneering, AstraZeneca, Amgen, CRICO and Manta Cares; receives institutional research funding from Pharmavite and Janssen; and serves as an Associate Editor at JAMA. articles.title: I Dumped Apple's Fucking Word List
articles.body:
~/Library/Keyboard/VulgarWordUsage.db
Lexicon.framework
Content note: this article prints the words uncensored, slurs included, because the article is about what Apple flags.
Nick posted this, I asked where it lives, and he answered. So I had Claude open mine.
$ sqlite3 -readonly ~/Library/Keyboard/VulgarWordUsage.db .schema CREATE TABLE properties (ROWID INTEGER PRIMARY KEY, key, value, UNIQUE (key)); CREATE TABLE IF NOT EXISTS "vword_usage" ( ROWID INTEGER PRIMARY KEY AUTOINCREMENT, app TEXT, -- app identifier recipient TEXT, -- recipient identifier vword TEXT, -- vulgar word word_reading TEXT, -- the reading form of a word (relevant for Japanese) usage_count INTEGER DEFAULT 0, last_use_timestamp REAL DEFAULT 0, -- last use timestamp (seconds since the reference date) journaled ); CREATE UNIQUE INDEX app_recipient_vword_word_reading_idx ON vword_usage(app, recipient, vword, word_reading);
So the keyboard can know that you say fuck in Messages to one particular friend, but not in Mail to your boss. The unique index is on (app, recipient, word, reading), so that is the granularity.
Mine is empty: no rows, a properties table holding only version = 2, and a modification date in April 2024.
At WWDC in June 2023, Craig Federighi announced the iOS 17 autocorrect rewrite with this line: "In those moments where you just want to type a ducking word, well, the keyboard will learn it, too." (TechCrunch, NPR)
These function names from the macOS shared library cache show how the keyboard uses the database:
TI::VulgarWordUsageDatabaseWrapper::set_current_app_id(CFString) TI::VulgarWordUsageDatabaseWrapper::set_current_recipient_ids(vector<string>) TI::VulgarWordUsageDatabaseWrapper::increment_usage_count(word, reading, recipients) TI::VulgarWordUsageDatabaseWrapper::decrement_usage_count(...) TI::VulgarWordUsageDatabaseWrapper::can_autocorrect(word, app, recipients) TI::VulgarWordUsageDatabaseWrapper::can_autocorrect_somewhere(word, reading) KB::FilterNonVulgarIfTopCandidateVulgar::filter_candidates(...) KB::Candidate::every_vulgar_word_is_allowlisted(VulgarWordUsageDatabaseWrapper*, ...)
Plus log strings like Passing recipient IDs to the vulgar word usage database wrapper; number of IDs: %lu.
A _KSUserWordsSynchroniser sharedAcrossLanguagesVulgarWordUsageValue symbol suggests it syncs between devices like your other learned words.
Claude tried to fill it, using agent-desktop to open a new TextEdit document and type well fuck this shit, damn it., first as a text insert, then as individual key presses. Nothing changed: no row, no log line, and the file's modification date stayed in 2024.
On Hacker News, swiftcoder reported that neither the database nor the ~/Library/Keyboard folder exists on their macOS Tahoe install. dr_pardee had the same problem, saw that macOS was trying to write the file and failing, and had Claude work out why. The prompt they used is in their gist.
The cause is a missing folder. AppleSpell, the background service behind autocorrect, opens ~/Library/Keyboard/VulgarWordUsage.db the first time a text field asks it for predictions in a given language. SQLite creates a database file when it's missing, but not the folder it lives in. Without ~/Library/Keyboard, the open fails with "no such file or directory", AppleSpell logs a com.apple.libsqlite3 error naming the path, and it carries on without the database. There's no visible error, so the feature stays off on that Mac without anyone noticing.
To get the file, create the folder, restart AppleSpell and type a sentence in a native app such as TextEdit:

articles.title: USDB: Scaling Storage for Next-Generation Recommender Systems at ByteDance
articles.body:
Computer Science > Databases
  [Submitted on 2 Nov 2026]
Title:USDB: Scaling Storage for Next-Generation Recommender Systems at ByteDance
View PDF HTML (experimental)
            Abstract:Recommendation models consume increasingly long, attribute-rich user histories, making small continuous updates and repeated large reads a central storage asymmetry. We present USDB, ByteDance's unified sequence storage practice for streaming and batch workloads. CascadeLSM time-based compaction stages materialize application-specific histories; differentiated replicas share persistent files; partial dumps reconstruct inference inputs from captured recent state and versioned history; and a hybrid columnar format accelerates projected reads. These designs reuse maintenance results across ingestion, inference, and training. Production migration records show 85.8% lower mean write latency, while normalized deployment accounting shows 42.1% lower infrastructure cost. Controlled comparisons with an Optimized RocksDB sequence baseline show faster long-history reads across projections and client loads. Aggregation pushdown sustains 8.5x the throughput of ordinary reads under a constrained receive budget. Production reconstruction and direct-file training results demonstrate how shared sequence maintenance supports fresh serving and repeated historical access.

articles.title: Arrows to arrows, categories to queries (2025)
articles.body:
Arrows to Arrows, Categories to Queries
I’ve had a little time off of work as of late, and been spending it in characteristically unwise ways. In particular, I’ve written a little programming language that compiles to SQL. I call it catlang. That’s not to say that I’ve written a new query language. It’s a programming language, whose compiler spits out one giant SELECT statement. When you run that query in postgres, you get the output of your program.
Why have I done this? Because I needed a funny compilation target to test out the actual features of the language, which is that its intermediary language is a bunch of abstract category theory nonsense. Which I’ll get to. But I’m sure you first want to see this bad boy in action.
Behold, the function that returns 100 regardless of what input you give it. But it does it with the equivalent of a while loop:
count : Int -> Int
count =
  x ->
    loop x
      i ->
        n <- join id id -< i
        z <- abs . (-) -< (n, 100)
        case z of
          inl _ -> inr . (+) -< (n, 1)
          inr _ -> inl -< n
If you’re familiar with arrow notation, you’ll notice the above looks kinda like one big proc block. This is not a coincidence (because nothing is a coincidence). I figured if I were to go through all of this work, we might as well get a working arrow desugarer out of the mix. But I digress; that’s a story for another time.
Anyway, what’s going on here is we have an arrow count, which takes a single argument x. We then loop, starting from the value of x. Inside the loop, we now have a new variable i, which we do some voodoo on to compute n—the current value of the loop variable. Then we subtract 100 from n, and take the absolute value. The abs function here is a bit odd; it returns Left (abs x) if the input was negative, and Right x otherwise. Then we branch on the output of abs, where Left and Right have been renamed inl and inr respectively. If n - 100 was less than zero, we find ourselves in the inl case, where we add 1 to n and wrap the whole thing in inr—which the loop interprets as “loop again with this new value.” Otherwise, n - 100 was non-negative, and so we can return n directly.
Is it roundabout? You bet! The obtuseness here is not directly a feature, I was just looking for conceptually simple things I could do which would be easy to desugar into category-theoretical stuff. Which brings us to the intermediary language. After desugaring the source syntax for count above, we’re left with this IL representation:
  id △ id
⨟ cochoice
    ( undist
    ⨟   ( (prj₁ ⨟ id ▽ id) △ id
          ⨟   ( prj₁ △ 100
              ⨟ (-)
              ⨟ abs
              )
            △ id
          ⨟ prj₁ △ id
          ⨟ dist
          ⨟   ( (prj₂ ⨟ prj₂ ⨟ prj₁) △ 1
              ⨟ (+)
              ⨟ inr
              )
            ▽ ( prj₂
              ⨟ prj₂
              ⨟ prj₁
              ⨟ inl
              )
        )
      △ prj₂
    ⨟ dist
    )
⨟ prj₁
We’ll discuss all of this momentarily, but for now, just let your eyes glaze over the pretty unicode.
The underlying idea here is that each of these remaining symbols has very simple and specific algebraic semantics. For example, A ⨟ B means “do A and pipe the result into B.” By giving a transformation from this categorical IL into other domains, it becomes trivial to compile catlang to all sorts of weird compilation targets. Like SQL.
You’re probably wondering what the generated SQL looks like. Take a peek if you dare.

                FROM

                FROM

                 (SELECT *

                   f0 AS f0, f1 AS f1, f2 AS f2, f3 AS f3, f4 AS f4, f5 AS f5, f6 AS f6

                    SELECT * FROM t35 AS _

                    ("f0" IS NOT NULL) AND ((("f1" IS NOT NULL) OR ("f2" IS NOT NULL)) AND (("f3" IS NOT NULL) AND ((("f4" IS NOT NULL) OR ("f5" IS NOT NULL)) AND ("f6" IS NOT NULL)))))

It’s not pretty, rather amazingly, running the above query in postgres 17 will in fact return a single row with a single column whose value is 100. And you’d better believe it does it by actually looping its way up to 100. If you don’t believe me, make the following change:
-     SELECT * FROM recursion ORDER BY step DESC LIMIT 1)
+     SELECT * FROM recursion ORDER BY step DESC)
which will instead return a row for each step of the iteration.
There are some obvious optimizations I could make to the generated SQL, but it didn’t seem worth my time, since that’s not the interesting part of the project.
What the Hell Is Going On?
Let’s take some time to discuss the underlying category theory here. I am by no means an expert, but what I have learned after a decade of bashing my head against this stuff is that a little goes a long way.
For our intents and purposes, we have types, and arrows (functions) between types. We always have the identity “do nothing arrow” id:
id  :: a ~> a
and we can compose arrows by lining up one end to another:1
(⨟) :: (a ~> b) -> (b ~> c) -> (a ~> c)
Unlike Haskell (or really any programming language, for that matter), we DO NOT have the notion of function application. That is, there is no arrow:
-- doesn't exist!
($) :: (a ~> b) -> a -> b
You can only compose arrows, you can’t apply them. That’s why we call these things “arrows” rather than “functions.”
There are a bundle of arrows for working with product types. The two projection functions correspond to fst and snd, taking individual components out of pairs:
prj₁ :: (a, b) ~> a
prj₂ :: (a, b) ~> b
How do we get things into pairs in the first place? We can use the “fork” operation, which takes two arrows computing b and c, and generates a new arrow which generates a pair of (b, c):
(△)  :: (a ~> b) -> (a ~> c) -> (a ~> (b, c))
If you’re coming from a Haskell background, it’s tempting to think of this operation merely as the (,) pair constructor. But you’ll notice from the type of the computation that there can be no data dependency between b and c, thus we are free to parallelize each side of the pair.
In category theory, the distinction between left and right sides of an arrow is rather arbitrary. This gives rise to a notion called duality where we can flip the arrows around, and get cool new behavior. If we dualize all of our product machinery, we get the coproduct machinery, where a coproduct of a and b is “either a or b, but definitely not both nor neither.”
Swapping the arrow direction of prj₁ and prj₂, and replacing (,) with Either gives us the following injections:
inl :: a ~> Either a b
inr :: b ~> Either a b
and the following “join” operation for eliminating coproducts:
(▽) :: (a ~> c) -> (b ~> c) -> (Either a b ~> c)
Again, coming from Haskell this is just the standard either function. It corresponds to a branch between one of two cases.
As you can see, with just these eight operations, we already have a tremendous amount of expressivity. We can express data dependencies via ⨟ and branching via ▽. With △ we automatically encode opportunities for parallelism, and gain the ability to build complicated data structures, with prj₁ and prj₂ allowing us to get the information back out of the data structures.
You’ll notice in the IL that there are no variable names anywhere to be found. The desugaring of the source language builds a stack (via the something to allocate △ id pattern), and replaces subsequent variable lookups with a series of projections on the stack to find the value again. On one hand, this makes the categorical IL rather hard to read, but it makes it very easy to re-target! Many domains do have a notion of grouping, but don’t have a native notion of naming.
For example, in an electronic circuit, I can have a ribbon of 32 wires which represents an Int32. If I have another ribbon of 32 wires, I can trivially route both wires into a 64-wire ribbon corresponding to a pair of (Int32, Int32).
By eliminating names before we get to the IL, it means no compiler backend ever needs to deal with names. They can just work on a stack representation, and are free to special-case optimize series of projections if they are able to.
Of particular interest to this discussion is how we desugar loops in catlang. The underlying primitive is cochoice:
cochoice :: (Either a c ~> Either b c) -> (a ~> b)
which magically turns an arrow on Eithers into an arrow without the eithers. We obviously must run that arrow on eithers. If that function returns inl, then we’re happy and we can just output that. But if the function returns inr, we have no choice but to pass it back in to the eithered arrow. In Haskell, cochoice is implemented as:
cochoiceHask :: (Either a c -> Either b c) -> a -> c
cochoiceHask f = go . Left
  where
    go :: Either a c -> b
    go eac =
      case f eac of
        Left b -> b
        Right c -> go (Right c)
which as you can see, will loop until f finally returns a Left. What’s neat about this formulation of a loop is that we can statically differentiate between our first and subsequent passes through the loop body. The first time through eac is Left, while for all other times it is Right. We don’t take advantage of it in the original count program, but how many times have you written loop code that needs to initialize something its first time through?
Compiling to SQL
So that’s the underlying theory behind the IL. How can we compile this to SQL now?
As alluded to before, we simply need to give SQL implementations for each of the operations in the intermediary language. As a simple example, id compiles to SELECT * FROM {}, where {} is the input of the arrow.
The hardest part here was working out a data representation. It seems obvious to encode each element of a product as a new column, but what do we do about coproducts? After much work thought, I decided to flatten out the coproducts. So, for example, the type:
(Int, Either Int Int)
would be represented as three columns:
( f1 INT NOT NULL
, f2 INT
, f3 INT
)
with the constraint that exactly one of f2 or f3 would be IS NOT NULL at any given point in time.
With this hammered out, almost everything else is pretty trivial. Composition corresponds to a nested query. Forks are CROSS JOINs which concatenate the columns of each sub-query. Joins are UNIONs, where we add a WHERE field IS NOT NULL clause to enforce we’re looking at the correct coproduct constructor.
Cochoice is the only really tricky thing, but it corresponds to a recursive CTE. Generating a recursive CTE table for the computation isn’t too hard, but getting the final value out of it was surprisingly tricky. The semantics of SQL tables is that they are multisets and come with an arbitrary greatest element. Which is to say, you need an column structured in a relevant way in order to query the final result. Due to some quirks in what postgres accepts, and in how I structured my queries, it was prohibitively hard to insert a “how many times have I looped” column and order by that. So instead I cheated and added a clock_timestamp() as step column which looks at the processor clock and ordered by that.
This is clearly a hack, and presumably will cause problems if I ever add some primitives which generate more than one row, but again, this is just for fun and who cares. Send me a pull request if you’re offended by my chicanery!
Stupid Directions To Go In the Future
I’ve run out of vacation time to work on this project, so I’m probably not going to get around to the meta-circular stupidity I was planning.
The compiler still needs a few string-crunching primitives (which are easy to add), but then it would be simple to write a little brainfuck interpreter in catlang. Which I could then compile to SQL. Now we’ve got a brainfuck interpreter running in postgres. Of course, this has been done by hand before, but to my knowledge, never via compilation.
There exist C to brainfuck compilers. And postgres is written in C. So in a move that would make Xzibit proud, we could run postgres in postgres. And of course, it would be fun to run brainfuck in brainfuck. That’d be a cool catlang backend if someone wanted to contribute such a thing.
Notes and Due Diligence and What Have You
I am not the first person to do anything like this. The source language of catlang is heavily inspired by Haskell’s arrow syntax, which in turn is essentially a desugaring algorithm for Arrows. Arrows are slightly the wrong abstraction because they require an operation arr :: (a -> b) -> (a ~> b)—which requires you to be able to embed Haskell functions in your category, something which is almost never possible.
Unfortunately, arrow syntax in Haskell desugars down to arr for almost everything it does, which in turn makes arrow notation effectively useless. In an ideal world, everything I described in this blog post would be a tiny little Haskell library, with arrow notation doing the heavy lifting. But that is just not the world we live in.
Nor am I the first person to notice that there are categorical semantics behind programming languages. I don’t actually know whom to cite on this one, but it is well-established folklore that the lambda calculus corresponds to cartesian-closed categories. The “closed” part of “cartesian-closed” means we have an operation eval :: (a ~> b, a) ~> b, but everyone and their dog has implemented the lambda calculus, so I thought it would be fun to see how far we can get without it. This is not a limitation on catlang’s turing completeness (since cochoice gives us everything we need.)
I’ve been thinking about writing a category-first programming language for the better part of a decade, ever since I read Compiling to Categories. That paper takes Haskell and desugars it back down to categories. I stole many of the tricks here from that paper.
Anyway. All of the code is available on github if you’re interested in taking a look. The repo isn’t up to my usual coding standards, for which you have my apologies. Of note is the template-haskell backend which can spit out Haskell code; meaning it wouldn’t be very hard to make a quasiquoter to compile catlang into what Haskell’s arrow desugaring ought to be. If there’s enough clamor for such a thing, I’ll see about turning this part into a library.
- When looking at the types of arrows in this essay, we make the distinction that ~> are arrows that we can write in catlang, while -> exist in the metatheory.↩︎

articles.title: Arrows to arrows, categories to queries (2025)
articles.body:
Arrows to Arrows, Categories to Queries
I’ve had a little time off of work as of late, and been spending it in characteristically unwise ways. In particular, I’ve written a little programming language that compiles to SQL. I call it catlang. That’s not to say that I’ve written a new query language. It’s a programming language, whose compiler spits out one giant SELECT statement. When you run that query in postgres, you get the output of your program.
Why have I done this? Because I needed a funny compilation target to test out the actual features of the language, which is that its intermediary language is a bunch of abstract category theory nonsense. Which I’ll get to. But I’m sure you first want to see this bad boy in action.
Behold, the function that returns 100 regardless of what input you give it. But it does it with the equivalent of a while loop:
count : Int -> Int
count =
  x ->
    loop x
      i ->
        n <- join id id -< i
        z <- abs . (-) -< (n, 100)
        case z of
          inl _ -> inr . (+) -< (n, 1)
          inr _ -> inl -< n
If you’re familiar with arrow notation, you’ll notice the above looks kinda like one big proc block. This is not a coincidence (because nothing is a coincidence). I figured if I were to go through all of this work, we might as well get a working arrow desugarer out of the mix. But I digress; that’s a story for another time.
Anyway, what’s going on here is we have an arrow count, which takes a single argument x. We then loop, starting from the value of x. Inside the loop, we now have a new variable i, which we do some voodoo on to compute n—the current value of the loop variable. Then we subtract 100 from n, and take the absolute value. The abs function here is a bit odd; it returns Left (abs x) if the input was negative, and Right x otherwise. Then we branch on the output of abs, where Left and Right have been renamed inl and inr respectively. If n - 100 was less than zero, we find ourselves in the inl case, where we add 1 to n and wrap the whole thing in inr—which the loop interprets as “loop again with this new value.” Otherwise, n - 100 was non-negative, and so we can return n directly.
Is it roundabout? You bet! The obtuseness here is not directly a feature, I was just looking for conceptually simple things I could do which would be easy to desugar into category-theoretical stuff. Which brings us to the intermediary language. After desugaring the source syntax for count above, we’re left with this IL representation:
  id △ id
⨟ cochoice
    ( undist
    ⨟   ( (prj₁ ⨟ id ▽ id) △ id
          ⨟   ( prj₁ △ 100
              ⨟ (-)
              ⨟ abs
              )
            △ id
          ⨟ prj₁ △ id
          ⨟ dist
          ⨟   ( (prj₂ ⨟ prj₂ ⨟ prj₁) △ 1
              ⨟ (+)
              ⨟ inr
              )
            ▽ ( prj₂
              ⨟ prj₂
              ⨟ prj₁
              ⨟ inl
              )
        )
      △ prj₂
    ⨟ dist
    )
⨟ prj₁
We’ll discuss all of this momentarily, but for now, just let your eyes glaze over the pretty unicode.
The underlying idea here is that each of these remaining symbols has very simple and specific algebraic semantics. For example, A ⨟ B means “do A and pipe the result into B.” By giving a transformation from this categorical IL into other domains, it becomes trivial to compile catlang to all sorts of weird compilation targets. Like SQL.
You’re probably wondering what the generated SQL looks like. Take a peek if you dare.

FROM

It’s not pretty, rather amazingly, running the above query in postgres 17 will in fact return a single row with a single column whose value is 100. And you’d better believe it does it by actually looping its way up to 100. If you don’t believe me, make the following change:
-     SELECT * FROM recursion ORDER BY step DESC LIMIT 1)
+     SELECT * FROM recursion ORDER BY step DESC)
which will instead return a row for each step of the iteration.
There are some obvious optimizations I could make to the generated SQL, but it didn’t seem worth my time, since that’s not the interesting part of the project.
What the Hell Is Going On?
Let’s take some time to discuss the underlying category theory here. I am by no means an expert, but what I have learned after a decade of bashing my head against this stuff is that a little goes a long way.
For our intents and purposes, we have types, and arrows (functions) between types. We always have the identity “do nothing arrow” id:
id  :: a ~> a
and we can compose arrows by lining up one end to another:1
(⨟) :: (a ~> b) -> (b ~> c) -> (a ~> c)
Unlike Haskell (or really any programming language, for that matter), we DO NOT have the notion of function application. That is, there is no arrow:
-- doesn't exist!
($) :: (a ~> b) -> a -> b
You can only compose arrows, you can’t apply them. That’s why we call these things “arrows” rather than “functions.”
There are a bundle of arrows for working with product types. The two projection functions correspond to fst and snd, taking individual components out of pairs:
prj₁ :: (a, b) ~> a
prj₂ :: (a, b) ~> b
How do we get things into pairs in the first place? We can use the “fork” operation, which takes two arrows computing b and c, and generates a new arrow which generates a pair of (b, c):
(△)  :: (a ~> b) -> (a ~> c) -> (a ~> (b, c))
If you’re coming from a Haskell background, it’s tempting to think of this operation merely as the (,) pair constructor. But you’ll notice from the type of the computation that there can be no data dependency between b and c, thus we are free to parallelize each side of the pair.
In category theory, the distinction between left and right sides of an arrow is rather arbitrary. This gives rise to a notion called duality where we can flip the arrows around, and get cool new behavior. If we dualize all of our product machinery, we get the coproduct machinery, where a coproduct of a and b is “either a or b, but definitely not both nor neither.”
Swapping the arrow direction of prj₁ and prj₂, and replacing (,) with Either gives us the following injections:
inl :: a ~> Either a b
inr :: b ~> Either a b
and the following “join” operation for eliminating coproducts:
(▽) :: (a ~> c) -> (b ~> c) -> (Either a b ~> c)
Again, coming from Haskell this is just the standard either function. It corresponds to a branch between one of two cases.
As you can see, with just these eight operations, we already have a tremendous amount of expressivity. We can express data dependencies via ⨟ and branching via ▽. With △ we automatically encode opportunities for parallelism, and gain the ability to build complicated data structures, with prj₁ and prj₂ allowing us to get the information back out of the data structures.
You’ll notice in the IL that there are no variable names anywhere to be found. The desugaring of the source language builds a stack (via the something to allocate △ id pattern), and replaces subsequent variable lookups with a series of projections on the stack to find the value again. On one hand, this makes the categorical IL rather hard to read, but it makes it very easy to re-target! Many domains do have a notion of grouping, but don’t have a native notion of naming.
For example, in an electronic circuit, I can have a ribbon of 32 wires which represents an Int32. If I have another ribbon of 32 wires, I can trivially route both wires into a 64-wire ribbon corresponding to a pair of (Int32, Int32).
By eliminating names before we get to the IL, it means no compiler backend ever needs to deal with names. They can just work on a stack representation, and are free to special-case optimize series of projections if they are able to.
Of particular interest to this discussion is how we desugar loops in catlang. The underlying primitive is cochoice:
cochoice :: (Either a c ~> Either b c) -> (a ~> b)
which magically turns an arrow on Eithers into an arrow without the eithers. We obviously must run that arrow on eithers. If that function returns inl, then we’re happy and we can just output that. But if the function returns inr, we have no choice but to pass it back in to the eithered arrow. In Haskell, cochoice is implemented as:
cochoiceHask :: (Either a c -> Either b c) -> a -> c
cochoiceHask f = go . Left
  where
    go :: Either a c -> b
    go eac =
      case f eac of
        Left b -> b
        Right c -> go (Right c)
which as you can see, will loop until f finally returns a Left. What’s neat about this formulation of a loop is that we can statically differentiate between our first and subsequent passes through the loop body. The first time through eac is Left, while for all other times it is Right. We don’t take advantage of it in the original count program, but how many times have you written loop code that needs to initialize something its first time through?
Compiling to SQL
So that’s the underlying theory behind the IL. How can we compile this to SQL now?
As alluded to before, we simply need to give SQL implementations for each of the operations in the intermediary language. As a simple example, id compiles to SELECT * FROM {}, where {} is the input of the arrow.
The hardest part here was working out a data representation. It seems obvious to encode each element of a product as a new column, but what do we do about coproducts? After much work thought, I decided to flatten out the coproducts. So, for example, the type:
(Int, Either Int Int)
would be represented as three columns:
( f1 INT NOT NULL
, f2 INT
, f3 INT
)
with the constraint that exactly one of f2 or f3 would be IS NOT NULL at any given point in time.
With this hammered out, almost everything else is pretty trivial. Composition corresponds to a nested query. Forks are CROSS JOINs which concatenate the columns of each sub-query. Joins are UNIONs, where we add a WHERE field IS NOT NULL clause to enforce we’re looking at the correct coproduct constructor.
Cochoice is the only really tricky thing, but it corresponds to a recursive CTE. Generating a recursive CTE table for the computation isn’t too hard, but getting the final value out of it was surprisingly tricky. The semantics of SQL tables is that they are multisets and come with an arbitrary greatest element. Which is to say, you need an column structured in a relevant way in order to query the final result. Due to some quirks in what postgres accepts, and in how I structured my queries, it was prohibitively hard to insert a “how many times have I looped” column and order by that. So instead I cheated and added a clock_timestamp() as step column which looks at the processor clock and ordered by that.
This is clearly a hack, and presumably will cause problems if I ever add some primitives which generate more than one row, but again, this is just for fun and who cares. Send me a pull request if you’re offended by my chicanery!
Stupid Directions To Go In the Future
I’ve run out of vacation time to work on this project, so I’m probably not going to get around to the meta-circular stupidity I was planning.
The compiler still needs a few string-crunching primitives (which are easy to add), but then it would be simple to write a little brainfuck interpreter in catlang. Which I could then compile to SQL. Now we’ve got a brainfuck interpreter running in postgres. Of course, this has been done by hand before, but to my knowledge, never via compilation.
There exist C to brainfuck compilers. And postgres is written in C. So in a move that would make Xzibit proud, we could run postgres in postgres. And of course, it would be fun to run brainfuck in brainfuck. That’d be a cool catlang backend if someone wanted to contribute such a thing.
Notes and Due Diligence and What Have You
I am not the first person to do anything like this. The source language of catlang is heavily inspired by Haskell’s arrow syntax, which in turn is essentially a desugaring algorithm for Arrows. Arrows are slightly the wrong abstraction because they require an operation arr :: (a -> b) -> (a ~> b)—which requires you to be able to embed Haskell functions in your category, something which is almost never possible.
Unfortunately, arrow syntax in Haskell desugars down to arr for almost everything it does, which in turn makes arrow notation effectively useless. In an ideal world, everything I described in this blog post would be a tiny little Haskell library, with arrow notation doing the heavy lifting. But that is just not the world we live in.
Nor am I the first person to notice that there are categorical semantics behind programming languages. I don’t actually know whom to cite on this one, but it is well-established folklore that the lambda calculus corresponds to cartesian-closed categories. The “closed” part of “cartesian-closed” means we have an operation eval :: (a ~> b, a) ~> b, but everyone and their dog has implemented the lambda calculus, so I thought it would be fun to see how far we can get without it. This is not a limitation on catlang’s turing completeness (since cochoice gives us everything we need.)
I’ve been thinking about writing a category-first programming language for the better part of a decade, ever since I read Compiling to Categories. That paper takes Haskell and desugars it back down to categories. I stole many of the tricks here from that paper.
Anyway. All of the code is available on github if you’re interested in taking a look. The repo isn’t up to my usual coding standards, for which you have my apologies. Of note is the template-haskell backend which can spit out Haskell code; meaning it wouldn’t be very hard to make a quasiquoter to compile catlang into what Haskell’s arrow desugaring ought to be. If there’s enough clamor for such a thing, I’ll see about turning this part into a library.
- When looking at the types of arrows in this essay, we make the distinction that ~> are arrows that we can write in catlang, while -> exist in the metatheory.↩︎

Title:The Little Book of Generative AI Foundations: An Intuitive Mathematical Primer
View PDF HTML (experimental)
            Abstract:This book provides a compact, derivation-oriented introduction to the mathematical foundations of modern generative artificial intelligence. Rather than surveying every recent architecture or implementation detail, it develops a coherent route through the ideas connecting major families of generative models, from PCA, probabilistic PCA, variational autoencoders, and diffusion models to normalising flows, autoregressive factorisations, GANs, Wasserstein GANs, and energy-based models. The aim is to make the structure of generative modelling more accessible without removing the mathematical substance needed to understand how these models are derived and related. The book is intended as a foundation-building primer for mathematically curious researchers, practitioners, and students.

Title:The Little Book of Generative AI Foundations: An Intuitive Mathematical Primer
View PDF HTML (experimental)
            Abstract:This book provides a compact, derivation-oriented introduction to the mathematical foundations of modern generative artificial intelligence. Rather than surveying every recent architecture or implementation detail, it develops a coherent route through the ideas connecting major families of generative models, from PCA, probabilistic PCA, variational autoencoders, and diffusion models to normalising flows, autoregressive factorisations, GANs, Wasserstein GANs, and energy-based models. The aim is to make the structure of generative modelling more accessible without removing the mathematical substance needed to understand how these models are derived and related. The book is intended as a foundation-building primer for mathematically curious researchers, practitioners, and students.
